rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s wording is deliberate; its style must be understood before interpreting the verse.
rows.anchor: Every word and every style of the Qur’ ān occupies a specific status without understanding which the verse cannot be correctly interpreted.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic negation can intensify denial: Imru’ al-Qays used laysa to mock a rival who lacked the courage to act.
rows.anchor: he does not have the courage do to do anything.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur’anic parallels say God is not in the least unjust, supporting this reading of the verse.
rows.anchor: God is not the slightest bit unjust. (4:40)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When a verse permits two readings, the one more congenial to and harmonious with the Qur’an should be preferred.
rows.anchor: that interpretation will be preferred which is more congenial and in harmony with the Qur’ ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is wholly beyond injustice and is unjust neither to the righteous nor to wrongdoers.
rows.anchor: He is beyond any semblance of injustice; He will neither be unjust to the righteous nor to the wrongdoers.

rows.speaker: al-Zamakhsharī
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī reads the verse to mean that oppressing obedient servants would be a great oppression, which God is not.
rows.anchor: only al-Zamakhshar ī32 has dealt with this issue.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi objects that ‘servants’ covers all people, pious and wicked, so the verse cannot be restricted to obedient servants.
rows.anchor: which is common to all human beings whether they are pious or wicked.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In context, God addresses people deserving Hell and tells them their fate is deserved, so He has not wronged them.
rows.anchor: they were told that they are facing a fate they were worthy of; God is not the slightest unjust to His people.

rows.speaker: some contemporary exegetes
rows.claim: They argue that a Creator’s injustice to His creation would be great oppression, which conflicts with God’s majesty.
rows.anchor: some contemporary exegetes in another way: Since if God Who is the creator is unjust to His creation

rows.speaker: the majority of our scholastics
rows.claim: The majority say every divine act is just, even placing the righteous in Hell or wrongdoers in Paradise; Islahi calls this view incorrect, though less wrong than the newer view.
rows.anchor: the majority of our scholastics are of the view that no act of God can be called unjust or oppressive

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God negates injustice through His justice, mercy, and wisdom, not on the ground that a Creator cannot be a great oppressor.
rows.anchor: it is through His attributes of justice, mercy and wisdom; He has nowhere negated them by saying that since He is the Creator

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: That rationale absurdly implies that even Pharaoh, Hāmān, Nimrod, and Shaddād cannot be called great oppressors, since they were not creators.
rows.anchor: if an act of oppression is from someone other than God then however extreme it may be, he cannot be called ẓallām

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi judges the old scholastic view wrong, though less wrong than the new view, and attributes both positions to ignorance of Arabic style.
rows.anchor: in spite of being incorrect is not as incorrect as the view of these new scholastics of this age.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell’s question about being filled and its answer may be a figurative portrayal or a real event.
rows.anchor: This question and answer could be a portrayal of the situation and also a real life matter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All created things understand God and answer Him; God can give speech to silent objects, as when criminals’ limbs testify.
rows.anchor: Whatever God has created understands His questions and also responds to Him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exchange conveys God’s self-sufficiency and intense wrath: filling Hell causes Him no hesitation, and more people would become its fuel.
rows.anchor: This question and answer is an expression of God’s self-sufficient nature and also of His intense wrath

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One possible reply has Hell answer furiously that it has ample room and should be given more inhabitants.
rows.anchor: if there are more, I have a lot of capacity; bring them forth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, overwhelmed by its many inhabitants, Hell may lose resolve and meekly ask whether more are coming.
rows.anchor: in this state of frailty it will ask if there are still more to come.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi prefers the furious reply because it matches God’s wrath and suits Hell’s vigorous obedience to His command.
rows.anchor: complete harmony between the poignant fury of God and the poignant fury of Hell

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s depiction of Hell’s vastness supports the furious reading and warns those who doubt it can hold multitudes.
rows.anchor: the vastness of Hell is mentioned in a style that it seems that those people are being warned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other passages depict Hell roaring, seething, and groaning as people are cast into it, reinforcing its fury.
rows.anchor: they shall hear it roaring and seething, as though bursting with rage

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Hell’s inhabitants, the righteous’ fate is described: Paradise is brought near as an honorific gift, sparing them a journey.
rows.anchor: they will be honoured and rewarded such that Paradise will be brought near them as a gift.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Paradise is already near; it is brought still nearer to honor its inhabitants, despite the wording suggesting a distance to cross.
rows.anchor: the fact of the matter is that it would be already near and to honour the inhabitants of Paradise will be brought further near them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase ‘ghayra baʿīd’ is a circumstantial accusative from ‘al-jannah’; although masculine, the form may grammatically qualify a feminine noun, as al-Zamakhsharī also allows.
rows.anchor: Al-Zamaksharī regards this to be technically possible and I agree with his opinion.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The words spoken at Paradise’s approach identify the promised reward of the prophets and messengers as now fulfilled.
rows.anchor: this is the reward for these people as promised to them by prophets and messengers of God; it is now being fulfilled.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Before the indefinite verb ‘tuʿadūn’ an incomplete verb is suppressed, understood as ‘mā kuntum tūʿadūn’.
rows.anchor: an incomplete verb is suppressed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘This’ refers to Paradise but, by interpretive convention, denotes its reward and gift; similar usage occurs in earlier sūrahs.
rows.anchor: This refers to Paradise; however, as per linguistic principles, it means reward and gift in accordance with interpretive rules.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description of Paradise’s recipients contrasts with the traits of Hell’s inmates described in verses 25–27.
rows.anchor: Earlier in verses 25-27, the character of the inmates of Hell has been delineated.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Awwāb’ and ‘ḥafīẓ’ describe the believer’s inner and outer self: a heart continually turned to God and deeds that respect His bounds.
rows.anchor: one of them relates to the heart and the other to the deeds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers need not renounce worldly life; their test is to remain awwāb and ḥafīẓ while living in the world, repenting when they exceed limits.
rows.anchor: forsaking this world is not necessary; in fact, his real test is that while leading this worldly life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Five daily prayers keep a believer turning to God, rooted in his center, and protected from Satan’s lure toward indecency; the Qur’an says prayer repels lewdness and evil.
rows.anchor: a believers trip to the mosque five times a dead is meant to keep alive in him this spirit to turn to God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In contrast, those destined for Hell doubt the Hereafter and seek other supports; Islahi calls these the root of all ailments.
rows.anchor: they have doubts about the Hereafter and instead of God have found other supports to cling to.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people of Paradise fear the unseen Merciful, are free of such doubts, rely on no other support, and come to God with hearts wholly inclined to Him.
rows.anchor: while not being able to see God, they fear him and since they did not find any other support for themselves

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The name ‘al-Raḥmān’ points to a wisdom of mercy: God must reward the devoted and punish rebellious people, or virtue and vice would be equal in His sight.
rows.anchor: it is the essential consequence of this attribute that the Almighty at last bring forth a day in which He reward people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an links the Day of Judgment to God’s self-decreed mercy and promise to gather humanity.
rows.anchor: God has decreed mercy for Himself, and shall definitely gather you on the Day of Judgement, (6:12)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers understood what God’s mercy requires, so they regarded the Day of Judgment as certain and remained vigilant.
rows.anchor: for this reason they regarded the Day of Judgement to be a certainty and remained vigilant about it.
